sentence: The router is a library inside the caller's own program [SYS-001].
A caller asks for a model group, a public model name [RSETUP-096].
On each try, it picks one deployment of that group: one provider's copy of the model [RSETUP-162].
This part builds the router from optional settings [RSETUP-277].
For the retry count and fallback cap, it takes your value, else a library-wide one, else a built-in default [RSETUP-031], [RSETUP-032].
It also decides which rule picks the deployment for each request [RSETUP-105].
Usually a chat request then goes into the retry and fallback loop [RSETUP-157], [RSETUP-190].
When this goes wrong, some bad settings stop the build with an error, and others are kept silently [RSETUP-257], [RSETUP-260].
A default queue priority set to any whole number makes every asynchronous chat request fail with an error [RSETUP-297].
The constructor reads its global settings once, builds the caches and registers callbacks on process-wide lists [RSETUP-277], [RSETUP-014], [RSETUP-049].

It validates the generic and content-policy fallback lists and, except for `"lar1"`, the top-level strategy, then builds that strategy's selector when it has one [RSETUP-257], [RSETUP-040], [RSETUP-045], [RSETUP-072].
Per request, the routing context takes a valid per-request override first, then the model's routing group, then the top-level strategy [RSETUP-105]-[RSETUP-108].
`completion` stamps bookkeeping into the request and hands it to the retry and fallback loop [RSETUP-157].
`acompletion` does too, except it diverts a prompt-management model, and sends a whole-number priority through the scheduler first [RSETUP-186], [RSETUP-187], [RSETUP-190].
router: the object that takes requests for model groups and picks a deployment for each try (`Router`)
model group: the public model name a caller asks for, shared by one or more deployments (`model_name`)
deployment: one provider's copy of a model, with its own credentials (`model_list`, `litellm_params`)
global setting: a library-wide value the router uses when your setting is unset, or your fallback list empty (`litellm.num_retries`, `litellm.fallbacks`)
retry count: how many more tries the loop makes inside the same group (`num_retries`)
fallback cap: the most fallback hops one request may take (`max_fallbacks`)
allowed failures: how many failures a deployment may have before it cools down (`allowed_fails`)
cooldown time: how long a failing deployment sits out (`cooldown_time`)
timeout: how long a provider call may run (`timeout`)
strategy: the rule that picks one deployment among the healthy ones (`routing_strategy`)
selector: the object that carries out a least-busy, usage-based, latency-based or cost-based strategy (`RouterStrategySelector`, `leastbusy_logger`)
routing group: a named set of model groups with its own strategy (`routing_groups`)
priority group: a routing group called by its own name; it can rank its members, and its strategy is random shuffle (`"priority"`)
per-request override: a strategy name sent with one request, used for that request only (`routing_strategy`)
routing context: the strategy and selector chosen for one request (`_get_routing_context`)
callback lists: process-wide lists of callbacks: objects the library notifies around every provider call (`litellm.callbacks`, `litellm.success_callback`)
pre-call check: an optional check that can filter deployments or raise an error before a call (`optional_pre_call_checks`)
discard: detaching a router from the process-wide lists (`discard()`)
blocking chat call: the chat method that makes its caller wait for the reply, with no queue (`completion`)
asynchronous chat call: the chat method a caller's program can wait on while doing other work; unlike the blocking chat call, it can queue requests (`acompletion`)
note: Fixed. The claim is now a contrast with `completion` only, so text-completion scheduling (RCALL-108, RCALL-092) no longer conflicts with it. RSETUP-190: 'When the effective priority is an `int`, the call goes through `schedule_acompletion` (priority queue)'. RSETUP-160: 'The sync path has no priority scheduling'. RSETUP-186 backs `acompletion` as the async chat entry. 'Can queue' fits, because queuing needs a priority (RSETUP-191), and the glossary's 'priority' row says so.

sentence: retry and fallback loop: the code that retries inside a group, then tries other groups (`function_with_fallbacks`, `async_function_with_fallbacks`)
metadata bucket: the request's metadata, which the router writes bookkeeping into in place (`metadata`)
fallback controls snapshot: a copy of the request's own fallback lists, kept so a broken stream re-enters the chain with them (`_mid_stream_fallback_controls`)
priority: a whole number that sends an asynchronous chat request through a queue (`priority`, `default_priority`)
scheduler: the queue that holds prioritised requests until their turn (`schedule_acompletion`)
prompt-management model: a model group served by one deployment whose model names a logging integration (`_is_prompt_management_model`)
attempt: one try against one deployment; each retry or fallback hop is a new attempt (`_completion`)
shadow traffic: background copies of a request sent to other groups; the caller's reply never waits for them (`silent_model`)
content-policy fallbacks: groups to try when a provider blocks a reply for its content (`content_policy_fallbacks`)
default fallbacks: catch-all fallback groups for any model, kept under one shared key (`default_fallbacks`)
environment gate: for a deployment that lists environments, the rule that loads it only on servers in one of them (`supported_environments`, `LITELLM_ENVIRONMENT`)
When you pass a Redis host without a port, no Redis is set up at construction, so the router runs in memory until Redis is attached later.

When a request's override is none of random shuffle, least-busy, the two usage-based strategies, latency-based or cost-based, for example `"lar1"`, a warning is logged and the model's normal strategy applies.
When a request names a priority group itself, with no valid override, candidates are all members' deployments, team-scoped when a team id is given; the strategy is random shuffle.
When a generic or content-policy fallback entry is not a mapping with exactly one key, construction raises a value error naming the first bad entry; context-window entries are never checked.
When a pre-call check name is unknown or misspelled, it is ignored with no warning.
When an asynchronous request has a truthy whole-number priority, it goes through the scheduler; a request priority of 0 counts as none, so the router's default applies.
When a blocking request names a deployment id, not a model name, as its model, the global pre-call checks are skipped.
When a reply is filtered; the router has content-policy fallbacks, but none for this group, the filtered reply returns, even with default fallbacks set.
When a deployment lists environments but `LITELLM_ENVIRONMENT` is unset, the environment gate raises a value error.
When a deployment's environment list is empty and `LITELLM_ENVIRONMENT` holds a valid value, the deployment is inactive everywhere.
For the retry count and fallback cap, a router checks three places in turn: your value, a library-wide setting, then a built-in default [RSETUP-031], [RSETUP-032].
It reads its library-wide settings once, when it is built, so changing one later leaves an existing router alone [RSETUP-277].
Some bad settings stop the build with an error; others are stored unchecked [RSETUP-257], [RSETUP-260].
An unknown constructor keyword raises a type error, so the proxy filters its settings against the valid names first [RSETUP-292], [RSETUP-059].
An explicit retry count or fallback cap wins even when it is 0, and the built-in defaults are 2 retries and 5 fallbacks [RSETUP-031], [RSETUP-032].
Allowed failures take your argument, else the global setting, which defaults to 3 [RSETUP-026].
Three settings treat 0 as unset [RSETUP-260].
A cooldown time of 0 becomes the 5-second default, a health staleness threshold of 0 becomes 600 seconds, and a timeout of 0 becomes the global request timeout [RSETUP-260].
The global request timeout defaults to 6000 seconds unless an environment variable sets it [RSETUP-033].
No numeric setting is range-checked, so a negative timeout is stored as given [RSETUP-260].
The client time-to-live setting is stored, but nothing reads it, so it has no effect [RSETUP-276].
At construction, the router sets up Redis only when you pass a Redis URL, or both a host and a port [RSETUP-006].
The proxy can attach Redis later, and does so only when the router has none [RSETUP-065], [RSETUP-067].
The router's caches for routing state, session bindings and prompt-cache pins share that one Redis client [RSETUP-014].
With Redis, cooldowns and usage are shared with every router on the same Redis; without it, they stay in one process [RSETUP-269].

Construction raises on the first bad setting, in this order: Redis setup, the deployment list, the fallback lists, the top-level strategy, the routing groups, then the retry and allowed-fails policies [RSETUP-257].
Each generic or content-policy fallback entry must be a mapping with exactly one key [RSETUP-040], [RSETUP-132], [RSETUP-133].
Validation does not check that key's value, whether the groups exist, or duplicates [RSETUP-134].
Each request's strategy, the rule that picks one deployment, comes from the first of three places that applies [RSETUP-105]-[RSETUP-108].
A valid strategy sent with the request wins [RSETUP-105].
Next comes a routing group: one the request names, or a non-priority group the model belongs to [RSETUP-106], [RSETUP-091].
Last comes the router's own strategy [RSETUP-108].
At construction the router validates its top-level strategy, except `"lar1"`, and builds its selector when the strategy has one [RSETUP-045], [RSETUP-071].
Five strategies get a selector: least-busy, both usage-based ones, latency-based and cost-based; random shuffle needs none [RSETUP-072].
Each routing group gets its own selector the same way [RSETUP-088].
Building groups is all-or-nothing, so a bad group leaves the previous groups in place [RSETUP-089].
The routing context resolves any alias before the group lookup [RSETUP-106].
An override other than the router's own strategy or random shuffle gets a selector, built on first use with empty settings [RSETUP-102], [RSETUP-072].
Members of a priority group are not mapped to it, so only a request that names the priority group itself, with no valid override, gets its random shuffle [RSETUP-091], [RSETUP-105], [RSETUP-107].
The request can name a rule: A request can carry its own strategy, and it wins over everything else when it is a supported strategy name [RSETUP-100], [RSETUP-105].
Bad overrides are ignored: Any other value is ignored with a warning, so a bad value stored on a key or team never fails the request [RSETUP-101].
Priority groups shuffle: Without a valid override, a request that names a priority group uses random shuffle, with no selector [RSETUP-105], [RSETUP-107].
Group members follow their group: A model that belongs to a non-priority routing group uses that group's strategy [RSETUP-106].
The router's rule comes last: A model in no group uses the router's own strategy [RSETUP-108].
Building a router adds its callbacks to the callback lists that every router in the same process shares [RSETUP-049], [RSETUP-078].
Those callbacks count usage and decide cooldowns after each provider call, through the library's logging rather than the call itself [SYS-003].
Detaching the router later removes most of them, but not all [RSETUP-062], [RSETUP-064].
Construction turns on the global setting that hides debug information, and creates a global response cache only when response caching is on and none exists [RSETUP-002], [RSETUP-012].

The default and group selectors double as logging callbacks: each joins the global callback list when that setting holds a list, and a least-busy one also joins the input list [RSETUP-078], [RSETUP-090].
A new pre-call check is dropped when the router already holds one of the same class [RSETUP-145].
Calling `discard()` removes the router from the set of live routers and strips every callback that is one of its own methods [RSETUP-062].
It also removes its recorded pre-call checks from the main callback list [RSETUP-063].
It leaves the selectors and the Slack alerting logger, which are registered as objects rather than as the router's own methods [RSETUP-064].
It also leaves the continuation-prefill check, which is never recorded among the router's pre-call checks [RSETUP-061].
A constructor that fails after registering its callbacks leaves them registered, and nothing can discard the half-built router [RSETUP-264], [RSETUP-301].
The asynchronous chat call records the request's details and bookkeeping [RSETUP-186].
In the usual case, it then sends the request to a priority queue or straight to the retry and fallback loop [RSETUP-187], [RSETUP-190].
The blocking chat call has no queue and sends no alerts [RSETUP-160].
`acompletion` writes the model, the messages, the stream setting and the per-attempt function into the request, then stamps the caller's metadata bucket in place [RSETUP-186], [RSETUP-268].
A prompt-management model goes to the prompt-management path and returns its result directly, with no snapshot, queue or duration report [RSETUP-187].
For every other model, the router stores the fallback controls snapshot, so a stream that breaks later re-enters the chain with the caller's original lists [RSETUP-189], [RSETUP-158].
The priority is the request's `priority` when truthy, else the router's `default_priority`, so a request priority of 0 counts as none [RSETUP-191].
A whole number goes through the scheduler; anything else goes straight to the retry and fallback loop [RSETUP-190].
A whole-number default breaks this path, because the scheduler call then lacks its priority and raises a type error [RSETUP-284].
On any failure, the same error is re-raised, and a background alert goes out only when Slack alerting is configured and the request did not come through the proxy [RSETUP-194], [RSETUP-195].
The request is stamped: The router writes the model and messages into the request and stamps the caller's metadata in place [RSETUP-186], [RSETUP-268].
Some models skip ahead: A model served by a single deployment that names a logging integration goes straight to the prompt-management path [RSETUP-187], [RSETUP-188].
Whole numbers wait in line: A whole-number priority on the request sends it to a queue, and a request priority of 0 counts as none [RSETUP-190], [RSETUP-191].
Queued requests come back: When its turn comes, the request re-enters the asynchronous chat call without its own priority [RSETUP-192].
Errors pass through unchanged: The caller gets the same error, and an alert goes out only when alerting is set up and the request did not come through the proxy [RSETUP-194], [RSETUP-195].
The blocking `completion` also skips the prompt-management path and the service-duration report, and re-raises loop errors as the same objects [RSETUP-160], [RSETUP-265].
Each blocking try picks one deployment, calls its provider and checks the reply [RSETUP-162], [RSETUP-169], [RSETUP-172].
When the provider blocked a reply for its content, a fallback group can answer instead, but only when the router's own settings allow it [RSETUP-171], [RSETUP-172].
The attempt retries nothing itself, and selection errors propagate to the loop [RSETUP-266], [RSETUP-162].
When the deployment names shadow targets, the attempt starts shadow traffic: one background thread per target, with a snapshot taken before credentials and tags are bound [RSETUP-165].
A shadow runs the router's full asynchronous path, its errors are only logged, and a shadow never launches shadows of its own [RSETUP-183], [RSETUP-184], [RSETUP-180].
The provider call merges the deployment's params, then the messages, caching setting and client, then the request's own keys, so request keys win [RSETUP-169].
A streamed reply has its first chunk read inside the attempt, so a stream that fails before that chunk raises inside the loop, where retries apply [RSETUP-174].

When a complete reply's first choice finished with `"content_filter"`, or it has no choices, the router's own settings decide whether the attempt raises a blocked-output error [RSETUP-171], [RSETUP-172].
When the router has content-policy fallbacks, they must give this group a target not yet attempted, and default fallbacks are not consulted [RSETUP-172].
Without them, only a `"*"` default fallback makes the rule raise [RSETUP-172].
Otherwise the filtered reply returns to the caller unchanged, with no error [RSETUP-172].
0s, caller: asks for group b; waiting
1s, group b: reply ends with content filter; checked by the rule
1s, group b: b's list names untried a; blocked-output error raised
2s, group a: loop sends request to a; answers normally
2s, caller: gets a's reply; one fallback attempted

A default queue priority set to any whole number, even 0, makes every asynchronous chat call fail, including calls that send no priority; each caller gets an error about a missing argument [RSETUP-297], [RSETUP-284].

Detaching a router leaves its selectors and Slack alerting on the shared lists [RSETUP-298]. The proxy does this for every request with its own router settings, so those lists keep growing and every later logging event visits them [RSETUP-298].

With default fallbacks set, building a router appends a catch-all entry to your fallback list, or to the library-wide one on every build [RSETUP-038], [RSETUP-299]. Any non-empty default parameters you pass are also changed in place [RSETUP-043].

Content-policy fallbacks sent with a single request never make the router act on a blocked reply by themselves; the router's own content-policy fallbacks or a catch-all default must trigger it [RSETUP-307], [RSETUP-303]. Otherwise the caller gets the blocked reply back [RSETUP-303].

Switching a latency-based router to least-busy through the strategy setup step, not the settings update, makes every later chat call on ungrouped models fail with an error saying no deployments are available [RSETUP-306].
Printing a deployment masks only the API key unless redaction is on, so other cloud secrets appear in clear text in an informational log line [RSETUP-150], [RSETUP-151].

Turning off the prompt-caching, model rate-limit or encrypted-content check on one router can silently remove it for another router in the same process that was built without a deployment list [RSETUP-309].
